newsitem.title: UK: Resilient pound has history of pre-election blues.
newsitem.headline: Resilient pound has history of pre-election blues.

text.p: Financial markets are shrugging off political risk ahead of Britain's general election as investors see victory by the opposition Labour Party as a foregone conclusion.
But analysts say such a sanguine view may be premature judging by sterling's performance during the run up to previous elections in the past 23 years.

The last six general elections were preceded by a tendency of the pound to weaken. On average, it fell by 2.6 percent against the mark although the pre-election decline has moderated a bit since the 1970s.

That might seem a small price to pay after sterling's near-20 percent rise against the mark in the past 12 months. But extreme examples, such as the 10 pfennig drop in the week before the 1983 poll, highlight sterling's propensity to go into freefall.

"Financial markets have so far taken a sanguine view of the general election but the view that political risk has been fully priced into sterling could yet prove dangerously premature," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
Coleman examined sterling's performance in the six weeks before and after general elections in the past 23 years.

To avoid the risks associated with comparing exchange rate movements between often arbitrary dates in a volatile, politically-driven trading environment, he looked at how closely its highs and lows occurred relative to each election date.
On each occasion, the low came much closer to the election than the high did. On average, sterling peaked 24 calendar days before an election, but hit a low only just six days before polling.
In 1983 and October 1974, last minute nerves dragged the pound to its low just a day before votes were cast.

One reason for last-minute volatility is that political risk tends to be priced into the markets very close to events such as elections, rather weeks than months. The British election has to be held by May 22.
So far, investors have been calm since Labour's long-standing and comfortable lead in opinion polls suggests a change in government would come as no surprise.

More important though is Labour leader Tony Blair's reshaping of the party towards the centre-ground. His pledges of economic and fiscal rectitude have raised expectations of little radical change in macroeconomic policy under a Labour government.

"We maintain that a Labour government would endeavour to gain the confidence of the financial markets by adopting a credible inflation target," said Peter von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS in London.

The pound's historical performance in the aftermath of elections is more mixed. In three out of the last six elections -- in 1983 and in both polls in 1974 -- sterling dropped sharply afterwards. In 1979 and 1992 it rose.

The recent loss of the government's parliamentary majority left the pound unfazed. But a reminder that sterling is not politically risk-proof was served by its slide when Prime Minister John Major called a leadership election in June 1995.
The pound dropped by over six pfennigs and almost four cents then, after being weakened already by weeks of intense party-infighting.

Sterling has risen to four-year highs recently amid expectations that base rates will go up by a total of three quarters of a percentage point by June 1997 from six percent at present to dampen buoyant consumer demand.
Combined with lingering expectations of rate cuts elsewhere in Europe, in particular Germany, sterling looks set to rally further, analysts said.

But despite Labour's apparently unsurmountable lead in the opinion polls it would be a mistake to write off the ruling Conservatives altogether. They could stage another recovery as in the 1992 election when opinion polls were a notoriously poor guide to the result.
A hung parliament, led by Labour without overall control, could bring new risks to sterling assets.
"This would be a very unusal outcome, and the fear of a follow-up election soon after the first would unsettle the markets," said Edmund Nonis, UK economist at Nikko Europe.
